profile.feeling: The golden-yellow spice of rice dishes and pickles — and, lately, of health drinks.

senses.def: turmeric — the plant (Curcuma longa) and its rhizome, fresh or dried and ground (mass noun)
curcumin, the yellow pigment of turmeric (Wiktionary)

examples.text: أَضَفْتُ قَلِيلًا مِنَ الْكُرْكُمِ إِلَى الْأَرُزِّ.
examples.tr: I added a little turmeric to the rice.
Turmeric gives food a yellow colour.
I bought fresh turmeric (root) at the market.
Many people drink milk with turmeric.

examples.text: يُطْلَقُ اسْمُ الْكُرْكُمِ أَيْضًا عَلَى الْمَادَّةِ الصَّفْرَاءِ الَّتِي تُلَوِّنُهُ.
examples.tr: The name kurkum is also given to the yellow substance that colours it (curcumin).

synonyms.nuance: Moroccan Arabic name of the spice (Wiktionary’s translation table, ḵarqūm)

etymology.text: Semitic cognates are Aramaic kurkmā, Akkadian kurkanū and Hebrew כַּרְכֹּם (karkom), but Wiktionary prefers a path via India, from Sanskrit कुङ्कुम (kuṅkuma); akin to Middle Persian kurkum and Ancient Greek κρόκος (krókos).

funFacts: The botanical name Curcuma is the Arabic word كُرْكُم, taken into Medieval Latin.
Hebrew כַּרְכֹּם (karkom), the saffron of the Song of Songs (4:14), is the same old word; turmeric itself is כּוּרְכּוּם (kurkum) in Modern Hebrew.
Greek κρόκος (krókos, crocus, saffron) is a relative of the word — Turkish uses a different, Persian name: zerdeçal (“yellow wood”).
pitfalls: Not saffron: saffron is زَعْفَرَان. Wiktionary even lists “Indian saffron” as a meaning of كُرْكُم, because the cheaper spice colours food the same way.
A mass noun without plural: one root is جَذْرُ كُرْكُمٍ, not *كُرْكُمَة.
subtleties: One word for the fresh rhizome and the dried powder; when the difference matters say كُرْكُمٌ طَازَجٌ (fresh) or كُرْكُمٌ مَطْحُونٌ (ground).
In chemistry texts كُرْكُم can mean the pigment curcumin (Wiktionary).

profile.feeling: Hairy leaves that taste of cucumber and sky-blue star-shaped flowers — a herb of the old Arab physicians.

senses.def: borage (Borago officinalis), its leaves and flowers (mass noun)
bugloss and viper’s bugloss — related plants of the genera Anchusa and Echium (Wiktionary)

examples.tr: Borage flowers are blue.

examples.text: تُؤْكَلُ أَوْرَاقُ الْحِمْحِمِ الصَّغِيرَةُ نِيئَةً فِي السَّلَطَةِ.
examples.tr: The young leaves of borage are eaten raw in salad.

examples.text: اِسْتَعْمَلَ الْأَطِبَّاءُ الْعَرَبُ الْحِمْحِمَ فِي أَدْوِيَةٍ تُسَبِّبُ الْعَرَقَ.
examples.tr: Arab physicians used borage in medicines that make one sweat.
I planted borage in the garden.

examples.text: يُطْلَقُ الْحِمْحِمُ فِي كُتُبِ النَّبَاتِ عَلَى أَنْوَاعٍ قَرِيبَةٍ مِنْ لِسَانِ الثَّوْرِ أَيْضًا.
examples.tr: In botanical books ḥimḥim is also used for related kinds of bugloss.

profile.synonymsNone: Wiktionary gives no other name for borage; لِسَانُ الثَّوْرِ (“ox tongue”) is its relative bugloss (Anchusa, Echium), and the alternative form حَمَاحِم is the same word.

etymology.text: From the root ح م م (“to become hot, to have a fever”; compare حَمَّام “bath”): Arab physicians used the leaves in medicines that make one sweat (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The same root gives حُمَّى (fever) and حَمَّام (bath), the source of Turkish hamam, Greek χαμάμ and English hammam.
English borage comes from Medieval Latin borrago, which Wiktionary derives either from Latin borra (“rough hair”) or from Arabic أَبُو الْعَرَقِ (“father of sweat”).
pitfalls: Not لِسَانُ الثَّوْرِ: Wiktionary gives that name to bugloss (Anchusa, Echium), a close relative with similar hairy leaves.
A botanist’s and herbalist’s word: in a greengrocer’s or a cookbook most Arabic speakers will not know it without a picture.
subtleties: Wiktionary uses حِمْحِم for borage and also for Anchusa and Echium; in a recipe it is borage.
A mass noun without plural: one plant = نَبْتَةُ حِمْحِمٍ.

profile.feeling: A dusty-green weed of fields and gardens — cooked like spinach in lean times and by foragers today.

senses.def: goosefoot, fat hen, lamb’s quarters (Chenopodium; mass noun)
orache (Atriplex) — Wiktionary gives this genus too

examples.text: السَّرْمَقُ نَبَاتٌ بَرِّيٌّ يَنْمُو فِي الْحُقُولِ.
examples.tr: Fat hen is a wild plant that grows in fields.
My grandmother cooked fat hen like spinach.
The young leaves of fat hen are eaten.

examples.text: يُطْلَقُ السَّرْمَقُ أَيْضًا عَلَى نَبَاتِ الْقَطَفِ.
examples.tr: sarmaq is also used for orache (qaṭaf).

examples.text: فِي بَعْضِ الْمَعَاجِمِ السَّرْمَقُ هُوَ الْقَطَفُ.
examples.tr: In some dictionaries sarmaq is orache.

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday name; Wiktionary gives سَرْمَق with the alternative forms سَرْمَج and سَرْمَة, which are spellings of the same word.

etymology.text: From Middle Persian *sarmag (“garden orache, Atriplex hortensis”), found in Classical Persian as سرمه (sarma) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Latin genus name Chenopodium is Greek for “goose foot” (χήν + πούς), after the shape of the leaves — hence English goosefoot.
pitfalls: Wiktionary uses سَرْمَق for goosefoot (Chenopodium) and for orache (Atriplex); for orache the usual word is قَطَف.
Few speakers know the word: in a shop or a recipe a description or the Latin name is safer.
subtleties: The Persian source meant garden orache, yet Wiktionary gives the Arabic word first for goosefoot (Chenopodium): the two leafy weeds look alike, and the name covers both.

profile.feeling: A sharp green paste from sushi bars — one dab too many and it shoots up the nose.

senses.def: wasabi — the Japanese plant (Eutrema japonicum) and the hot green paste made from its grated rhizome (mass noun, indeclinable)

examples.tr: Sushi is served with wasabi and ginger.
Wasabi is very hot.
I bought a tube of wasabi at the shop.

profile.synonymsNone: No native word: the Japanese name is borrowed; only its spelling varies (واسابي, وسابي).

etymology.text: Borrowed from Japanese 山葵 (wasabi). Wiktionary has no Arabic entry; its translation table gives وَسَابِي, masculine.

funFacts: Most “wasabi” sold outside Japan is horseradish coloured green — in Arabic terms فُجْلٌ حَارٌّ (node veg.2a) rather than real wasabi.
pitfalls: The spelling is not fixed: this course writes واسابي, with long ā, as it is usually written; Wiktionary’s translation table has وَسَابِي.
Indeclinable (ends in -ī): no case endings, only الـ for “the”: الْوَاسَابِي.

profile.feeling: Sour pink stalks for European pies and jams — and, in the Arabic tradition, a bitter root from the apothecary.

senses.def: rhubarb (Rheum): the plant, its sour edible stalks and its medicinal root (mass noun)

examples.tr: Rhubarb is very sour.
I made rhubarb jam with sugar.

examples.text: لَا تَأْكُلْ أَوْرَاقَ الرَّاوَنْدِ فَهِيَ سَامَّةٌ.
examples.tr: Don’t eat rhubarb leaves — they are poisonous.

examples.text: اُسْتُعْمِلَ جَذْرُ الرَّاوَنْدِ دَوَاءً مُنْذُ الْقِدَمِ.
examples.tr: Rhubarb root has been used as a medicine since ancient times.

synonyms.nuance: the wild Syrian rhubarb (Rheum ribes) of the region’s mountains, whose stalks are eaten; Wiktionary also gives it for currants (Ribes)

funFacts: Turkish ravent and Russian ревень (revenʹ) come from the same Persian word; English rhubarb and German Rhabarber go back instead to Medieval Latin rheubarbarum, “foreign rhubarb”.
pitfalls: Only the stalks are eaten: the leaves are poisonous (oxalic acid).
رِيبَاس is not simply a synonym: Wiktionary gives it for the wild Syrian rhubarb and also for currants.
subtleties: In older Arabic texts رَاوَنْد is first of all the dried medicinal root (a purgative traded from Central and East Asia), not a food.

profile.feeling: A pine-sharp cousin of ginger — Thai curries today, the herbalist’s drawer in the old Arab world.

senses.def: galangal (Alpinia, especially Alpinia officinarum), its aromatic rhizome (mass noun)

examples.tr: Galangal looks like ginger.

examples.text: أَضِفْ شَرَائِحَ مِنَ الْخَوْلَنْجَانِ إِلَى الْحَسَاءِ.
examples.tr: Add slices of galangal to the soup.
Ground galangal is sold at the herbalist’s.

synonyms.nuance: the same word vocalized with ū (ḵūlanjān); Wiktionary gives both

etymology.text: From Persian قولنجان (qulanjân), from Sanskrit कुलञ्जन (kulañjana), possibly from Chinese 高良薑 (gāoliángjiāng) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: English galangal came from this Arabic word through Old French — and if Wiktionary’s guess is right, the chain starts in Chinese 高良薑.
pitfalls: Not ginger: galangal is harder, woodier and more peppery; زَنْجَبِيل does not replace it one for one.
subtleties: Two vocalizations are standard: خَوْلَنْجَان (ḵawlanjān) and خُولَنْجَان (ḵūlanjān) (Wiktionary).

profile.feeling: Silvery, salty leaves of a desert shrub — grazing for camels, a wild green for people.

senses.def: orache, saltbush (Atriplex): the wild shrubs and the garden orache (mass noun)

examples.tr: Saltbush grows on salty land.
Orache leaves taste a little salty.
Orache leaves are cooked like spinach.
Camels eat saltbush.

synonyms.nuance: older botanical name, from Persian “garden orache”; Wiktionary gives it for goosefoot (Chenopodium) as well

etymology.text: Wiktionary: the saltbush name must come from Classical Syriac ܩܛܦܐ (qaṭəp̄ā, “saltbush”), whose vocalization it mirrors; it only looks like the verb قَطَفَ (“to pick”).

funFacts: Job 30:4 describes starving men “who pluck saltbush” — הַקֹּטְפִים מַלּוּחַ — with the Hebrew twin of the verb قَطَفَ.
pitfalls: Only the vowels separate قَطَف (qaṭaf, saltbush) from قَطْف (qaṭf, picking) and قِطْف (qiṭf, a bunch) (Wiktionary).
subtleties: Wiktionary gives the whole genus Atriplex: wild desert saltbushes and the cultivated garden orache share the name.

profile.feeling: Old-fashioned soap: salty marsh plants whose ash washed hands and clothes for centuries.

senses.def: glasswort, saltwort — salt-loving plants of the amaranth family, among them Salicornia (Wiktionary; mass noun)
potash — the alkaline ash of these plants, used for washing (Wiktionary)

examples.text: يَنْمُو الْأُشْنَانُ عَلَى شَوَاطِئِ الْبَحْرِ وَفِي السِّبَاخِ.
examples.tr: Glasswort grows on seashores and in salt marshes.
Glasswort stems are salty and are eaten pickled.
People used to wash their hands with ushnan.

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday modern word for the vegetable; modern texts tend to use the Latin genus name Salicornia or a description.

etymology.text: Borrowed from Classical Persian اُشْنَان (ušnān) or its Middle Persian ancestor; related to Arabic أُشْنَة (“moss, lichen”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The ash of such plants was also called al-qily in Arabic — the origin of English alkali.
English glasswort tells the same story: the ash was used to make glass, and soap.
pitfalls: A classical word for a group of salt plants (Salsola, Salicornia, Anabasis … in Wiktionary), not a greengrocer’s name for the sea vegetable.
subtleties: In classical texts the word mostly means the washing agent, not a food: the same word names the plant and its ash.

profile.feeling: The white, crunchy, faintly sweet core of a date palm — a rare treat, because taking it kills the palm.

senses.def: heart of palm, palm cabbage — the edible core and growing bud of a palm, above all the date palm; plural جُمَّارَات

examples.tr: We ate heart of palm with dates.
Heart of palm is white and tender.
I bought a tin of hearts of palm.

examples.text: كُنَّا عِنْدَ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَأُتِيَ بِجُمَّارٍ.
examples.tr: We were with the Prophet, and some heart of palm was brought to him.

collocations.tr: a tin of hearts of palm

phrases.text: كُنَّا عِنْدَ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَأُتِيَ بِجُمَّارٍ
phrases.tr: We were with the Prophet, and some heart of palm was brought to him
phrases.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Kitāb al-ʿIlm (ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar)
phrases.meaning: The opening of the hadith in which the Prophet, with heart of palm brought to him, asks which tree is like a Muslim — the date palm.

synonyms.nuance: “heart”: Wiktionary’s translation table also gives قَلْب (qalb, qilb, qulb) for the palm heart — the general word, not specific

etymology.text: Wiktionary: the alternative form جَامُور (jāmūr) shows Aramaic borrowing, like كَافُور (“bract of the date-palm inflorescence”) and تَمْر (“date”).

funFacts: In the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, heart of palm was brought to the Prophet and he asked his companions which tree is like a Muslim: the answer was the date palm.
pitfalls: A date palm has only one growing point: cutting out the heart kills the tree, so جُمَّار of date palms is a by-product of felling.
Do not translate “heart of palm” word for word as قَلْبُ النَّخْلَةِ in a recipe — the word is جُمَّار.
subtleties: Countable (plural جُمَّارَات, Wiktionary) for pieces or palms, but as food the singular is used like a mass noun: أَكَلْنَا الْجُمَّارَ.
Wiktionary also lists the alternative forms جُمَّارَة and جَامُور.

profile.feeling: A leafy wild green of the amaranth family — a weed to farmers, spinach to foragers.

senses.def: amaranth greens, blite (Amaranthus blitum) and similar leafy plants of the amaranth family — Wiktionary: identified “not conclusively” (mass noun)

examples.tr: Amaranth is a wild plant whose leaves are eaten.
We cooked the amaranth greens with garlic and oil.
I picked some amaranth at the edge of the field.

synonyms.nuance: obsolete form of the same word (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: From Persian تاج خروس (tâj xorus, “amaranth”, literally “cockscomb”), from Middle Persian xrōs (“rooster”) + tāg (“crown, comb”); cognate with Jewish Palestinian Aramaic ירבוז (yarbūz) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Modern Hebrew יַרְבּוּז (yarbuz) is the everyday word for amaranth — the same old name, from the Aramaic form.
The Persian source means “rooster’s crown”, the same picture as English cockscomb, an ornamental relative.
pitfalls: Wiktionary marks the identification as not conclusive: old texts use the name for several leafy plants of the amaranth family, goosefoots included.
subtleties: Wiktionary lists the alternative forms يَرْبُوز (obsolete), أَرْبُوز and جَرْمُوز.
